extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and newsroom staff reporting on disability and mental-health topics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists on appropriate language, terminology and sourcing when reporting about people with disabilities, mental illness and related conditions. Emphasizes people-first language, when to report diagnoses, preferred/avoided terms, and brief background on conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dementia
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to someone as having dementia only if the information is relevant* to the story and a licensed medical professional has formally diagnosed the person. Use people-first language when describing someone with dementia, such as “a person with dementia.” Avoid describing someone as being demented or senile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, reference the specific disease, such as “someone with Huntington’s disease.” When referencing Huntington’s disease or Parkinson’s disease, do not shorten to Huntington’s or “Parkinson’s.” AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depression
rubrics_metrics.description: Depression (proper name: major depressive disorder) is characterized by loss of interest, persistent fatigue, difficulty concentrating/deciding, feelings of emptiness or hopelessness and abnormal eating habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having depression only if the information is relevant* to the story and if the person has been formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Specify the type of disorder if known. The terms depressed, depressing, and depressive are acceptable in other contexts when the person does not have a medically diagnosed condition. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental disabilities are conditions that arise due to impairment in physical, learning, language or behavior areas, begin during the developmental period and usually last throughout a person’s lifetime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While it is acceptable to use the term developmental disabilities, it is preferable to use the name of the specific disability whenever possible. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled / disability (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability and disabled generally describe functional limitations that affect major life activities (walking, lifting, learning, breathing, etc.). Various laws define disability differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing an individual, do not reference his or her disability unless it is clearly pertinent to the story. If pertinent, use people-first language (e.g., “The writer, who has a disability” vs. “the disabled writer”). When possible, refer to a person’s specific condition. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) / multiple personality disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissociative identity disorder is characterized by the emergence of two or more distinct personality states (alters) that can show different speech, mannerisms, attitudes, gender identities and even physical characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having dissociative identity disorder only if the information is relevant* to the story and if the person has been formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use the term dissociative identity disorder, not multiple personality disorder, and avoid the acronym DID. Use people-first language, e.g., “a person with dissociative identity disorder.” AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Down syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Down syndrome is a congenital condition caused by an extra full or partial copy of chromosome 21, and is characterized by a number of physical and cognitive symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper term is Down syndrome (not Down's syndrome). Use people-first language: “a person with Down syndrome” or “has Down syndrome.” Avoid terms like “suffers from” or “afflicted with.” Terms such as intellectually disabled, developmentally disabled, cognitive disability and intellectual disability are acceptable in people-first contexts, but it is more accurate to refer specifically to Down syndrome when that is the diagnosis. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dwarf / little person / midget / short stature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwarfism is a medical/genetic condition resulting in stature below 4'10"; 'midget' was used historically for a proportionate unusually short person and is now widely considered derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only refer to a person’s short stature if it is relevant* to the story. Ask people which term they prefer. Avoid the term dwarf unless used in a quote or medical diagnosis. Avoid 'vertically challenged' and 'midget.' Little People of America recommends 'short stature,' 'little person' or 'someone with dwarfism.' AP style: Dwarf is the preferred medical term; midget is offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dyslexia / dyslexic
rubrics_metrics.description: Dyslexia is a learning disability characterized by problems identifying speech sounds and connecting them to letters/words, causing difficulties with spelling, reading and word pronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having dyslexia only if the information is relevant* to the story and if the person has been formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use people-first language (state that someone has dyslexia rather than calling them 'a dyslexic person'). Avoid using 'dyslexic' as a noun. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilepsy / epileptic fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures; manifestations and severity vary by individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having epilepsy only if the information is relevant* to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use people-first language (someone has epilepsy or has been diagnosed with epilepsy) rather than calling them an 'epileptic.' Use the term 'seizure' for the brief manifestation of symptoms; avoid 'fit' or 'epileptic fit.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handicap / handicapped
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically used term defined as a condition that restricts a person’s ability to function physically, mentally or socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not describe a person as handicapped unless it is central to the story. Avoid using 'handicap' and 'handicapped' when describing a person; instead refer to the person’s specific condition. These terms remain in use when citing laws/regulations/places (e.g., handicapped parking), though many prefer 'accessible parking.' Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard of hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to people who have mild to moderate hearing loss that may or may not be corrected with amplification and who usually use speech to communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard of hearing is almost always acceptable; however, use the term the person prefers. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing impaired / hearing impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: General terms describing a range of hearing loss from partial to complete; disliked by many because they frame a person in terms of deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those with total hearing loss, 'deaf' is acceptable; for others, 'partial hearing loss' or 'partially deaf' is preferred. It is best to ask the person which term they prefer. AP style: Uses 'deaf' for total loss and recommends 'partial hearing loss' or 'partially deaf' for others; does not address 'hearing impaired.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantile paralysis / polio
rubrics_metrics.description: Infantile paralysis was used historically for poliomyelitis (polio); symptoms include muscle weakness and paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term 'polio' rather than 'infantile paralysis.' Prefer phrasing like 'He had polio as a child' or 'She contracted polio as an adult' rather than 'He suffers from polio' or 'He is a victim of polio.' AP style: Preferred word is 'polio.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury / injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Injury commonly describes harm, damage or impairment resulting from an accident or other event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to injuries as being 'sustained' or 'received,' not 'suffered,' unless the person prefers 'suffered.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane / insanity / mentally deranged / psychopathology
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as 'insane' and 'mentally deranged' are commonly used informally to denote mental instability but can be offensive; medically, 'mental disorder' or 'psychopathology' are preferred, and 'insanity' is a legal question in criminal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'mental illness' or 'mental disorder' instead of 'insane' or 'mentally deranged,' except in quotes or when referring to a criminal defense. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insane asylum / mental health hospital / psychiatric hospital
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical term 'insane asylum' described hospitals caring for people with mental illnesses for long periods; term is objectionable and outdated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'mental health hospital' or 'psychiatric hospital' to describe medical facilities devoted to treating people with mental disabilities. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual disabilities / intellectually disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual disability involves significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior; typically develops before age 18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language: 'a person with an intellectual disability' rather than 'an intellectually disabled person.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: An archaic term defined as a person made weak or disabled by illness or injury; widely viewed as offensive because it implies lack of abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'invalid' to describe a person with a disability except when quoting someone. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lame
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used to describe difficulty walking due to leg injury; also used colloquially as a synonym for 'weak' in a pejorative way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'lame' to describe a person with a disability except when quoting someone. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little person / little people
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference to entry on 'Dwarf, little person/people/midget/short stature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the guidance under 'Dwarf, little person/people/midget/short stature' regarding relevance, preferred terms, and asking individuals which terms they prefer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental illness / mental disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella term for conditions affecting how individuals act, think, feel or perceive; includes anxiety disorders, mood disorders and schizophrenia, with wide variance in severity and symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to an individual’s mental illness only when relevant* to the story and the diagnosis comes from a proper source. Whenever possible, specify the specific illness rather than using the general term. Always use people-first language. Use quotes when officials or family members use terms such as 'a history of mental illness' and indicate when a diagnosis has not been confirmed. Avoid gratuitously linking mental illness and violent crime; ensure sources have authority to speak about a suspect’s mental-health history. Do not use mental-health terms to describe non-health issues (e.g., calling a show 'schizophrenic'). Conforms to AP style guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental health professionals / 'shrink'
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple types of mental health professionals (psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, psychologist, psychotherapist) with different training and roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the professional how he or she should be identified based on formal training. Avoid using the word 'shrink' except in quotes. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms: mentally retarded, retard, mental retardation
rubrics_metrics.description: These terms were once common but are now considered outdated and offensive; 'Rosa's Law' (2010) replaced 'mental retardation' with 'intellectual disability' in many government contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always try to specify the type of disability being referenced. Otherwise, terms such as 'mental disability,' 'intellectual disability,' and 'developmental disability' are acceptable. Use people-first language (e.g., 'people with mental disabilities' rather than 'the mentally disabled'). Outdated terms may be used only in historical context with attribution or explanation. AP style: 'Mentally retarded' should be avoided; AP suggests terms such as 'mentally disabled,' 'intellectually disabled' and 'developmentally disabled.' The NCDJ prefers 'a person with a mental disability.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Midget
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference to 'Dwarf, little person/people/midget/short stature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the guidance under 'Dwarf, little person/people/midget/short stature' — 'midget' is considered offensive and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mongoloid
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically used in the late 19th century to refer to people with Down syndrome; term derived from comparisons to racial labels and is highly derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always avoid the use of 'mongoloid' to refer to someone with Down syndrome. See Down syndrome entry. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple personality disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: See entry on Dissociative identity disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'dissociative identity disorder' rather than 'multiple personality disorder'; see DID guidance about diagnosis, relevance and people-first language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
rubrics_metrics.description: MS is a disease of the central nervous system that disrupts information flow in the brain/body; symptoms vary and may include trouble walking, numbness and vision problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to describe a person as 'someone with multiple sclerosis,' followed by a short explanation of how the disease is manifested in that person. Avoid saying a person 'suffers from' or 'is afflicted with' the disease. 'MS' is acceptable on second reference. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular dystrophy (MD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscular dystrophy refers to any of more than 30 genetic diseases characterized by progressive muscle weakness and degeneration; onset varies from infancy to later life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to describe a person as 'someone with muscular dystrophy,' followed by a short explanation of what the condition entails. Avoid saying a person 'suffers from' or 'is afflicted with' the disease. 'MD' is acceptable on second reference. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to refer to someone who does not have a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Non-disabled' or 'does not have a disability' are acceptable when referring to people who do not identify as having a disability. In general, avoid using 'able-bodied.' AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCD is an anxiety disorder characterized by unreasonable thoughts and fears leading to repetitive, ritualized behaviors or compulsions; people may exhibit obsessions, compulsions, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having OCD only if the information is relevant* to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a reputable source. Do not use 'OCD' as an adjective for someone who obsesses over certain things but lacks a formal diagnosis. Use 'obsessive-compulsive disorder' on first reference; 'OCD' is acceptable on second reference. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraplegia / paraplegic
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraplegia is impairment or loss of movement in the lower extremities and torso, typically caused by spinal cord or brain injury. Referring to someone as 'a paraplegic' can imply the condition defines them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid referring to an individual as a 'paraplegic.' Instead, say the person 'has paraplegia.' If a person self-identifies as 'a para,' use that in quotes. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: (Partial) hearing loss / partially deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard of hearing is the most common term for those with mild to moderate hearing loss; partial hearing loss or partially deaf are other descriptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the individual what term he or she prefers. Otherwise, 'hard of hearing' is almost always acceptable. AP style: Recommends using 'partial hearing loss' or 'partially deaf' for those with some hearing loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: People-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: People-first language avoids defining a person in terms of a disability by placing reference to the disability after the reference to the person (e.g., 'A person with a disability' vs. 'the disabled person').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language whenever possible. Note that some organizations acknowledge people-first phrasing can be awkward and allow deviations when the only alternative is awkward sentence structure. Refer to CDC guidance on people-first language as needed. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prelingually deaf / postlingually deaf / late-deafened
rubrics_metrics.description: Prelingually deaf refers to individuals born deaf or becoming deaf prior to learning to speak; postlingually deaf/late-deafened describes those who lost hearing after learning to speak a language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are acceptable, although explanation may be required for a general audience. AP style: Not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTSD is an anxiety disorder generally caused by experiencing an extremely traumatic event; symptoms may include reliving the event, avoidance, negative emotions and physical symptoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having PTSD only if the information is relevant* to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a reputable source. 'Post-traumatic stress disorder' is correct on first reference; use 'PTSD' on second reference. The term 'flashback' may be used to denote reliving a triggering event. AP style: Not addressed.
